Atlas by GiveCentral · Flagship Case Study

Redesigning the donor-management experience.

B2B SaaSProduct DesignUX StrategyDesign System

How I turned a sprawling, 18-module fundraising CRM into one system where teams can find, understand, and act on donor information faster — across the whole product, from the dashboard to reporting to an AI assistant.

RoleProduct Designer (lead)
TeamPM · Engineers · Design Manager
Timeline~4 months, then ongoing
My contributionResearch · UX · UI · Prototyping · Design System
PlatformWeb / SaaS (+ a mobile companion)
UsersFundraising & operations teams at Catholic dioceses

Scope at a glance — the modules this redesign touched: Dashboard · Donors · Gifts & Pledges · Campaigns (Funds, Appeals) · Reports · Prospect Pipeline · Tasks & Reminders · Communications · Events · Volunteers · Guru AI · Analytics · Users & Roles · Tags & Segments · Integrations · Smart Triggers · Sync · Location Portal.

02 — THE PROBLEM

Donor information lived in too many places

Fundraising teams were managing donor information across separate workflows — a list here, a profile there, payments somewhere else — so understanding a donor's history and taking the next action meant repeatedly switching contexts and losing the thread.

Current workflow Search → Donor list → Profile → (back) → Payments → (back) → Timeline → Action ↑ context lost ↑ context lost ↑ context lost ↑ re-orient

Evidence (stakeholder-driven redesign): this was framed from support themes, stakeholder interviews, and the observable workflow — not a formal research study. I'm explicit about that.

"I'm digging through three screens just to remember what this donor gave last year before I call them."
— Development Director
"By the time I log the visit at my desk, half the context is gone."
— Gift Officer
03 — BUSINESS CONTEXT

Business → user → design

Business goal

Efficiency & a platform to grow on

Make donor management efficient and lay a foundation (tokens, components, IA) that future fundraising workflows can be built on quickly.

User goal

Context, then action

Quickly understand a donor's situation and take the right next step — without hunting across screens.

Design goal

Less navigation, same depth

Cut unnecessary navigation while keeping complex donor and compliance information fully accessible.

Why it matters

Retention is revenue

Faster, better-informed stewardship protects donor retention — the compounding lever of fundraising.

05 — RESEARCH & DISCOVERY

Three things I needed to understand

01

User behavior

How do teams actually complete the find → understand → act loop today?

02

Pain points

Where exactly do they lose context or get blocked?

03

Business requirements

Which information and actions are non-negotiable (compliance, receipting, permissions)?

The most useful output wasn't the research itself — it was turning each finding into a design implication:

Finding: users constantly switch between a donor's profile and their payment/giving history.↓Implication: giving context must live inside the donor workspace, not a screen away.
Finding: people re-run the same reports weekly and export to Excel to answer basic questions.↓Implication: make reporting self-serve and repeatable (saved views), and let AI answer in plain English.
Finding: the same donor gives to several legal entities; staff couldn't see the whole person safely.↓Implication: global identity, entity-gated financials.
06 — KEY INSIGHTS

Four insights that shaped everything

01

Users need context before action — not a wall of metrics.

02

The old navigation separated information users need together.

03

Search is a primary workflow, not just a nav utility.

04

Advanced/admin depth shouldn't compete with primary tasks.

07 — DEFINE THE PROBLEM

The question I designed against

How might we help fundraising teams understand donor context and take action — without navigating across multiple screens — while keeping an 18-module product coherent and compliant?

Success means

  • Reduce unnecessary navigation
  • Preserve important context at the moment of action
  • Improve information hierarchy
  • Support multiple roles (officer, admin, finance, leadership)
  • Scale to future workflows without redrawing every screen
08 — EXPLORE SOLUTIONS

Three directions, one decision

ConceptAdvantageProblem
A · Tabbed workspaceFamiliar, low-riskContext still fragmented across tabs
B · Split-screen detailEfficient side-by-sideLimited screen space for dense data
C · Unified donor workspaceStrong context in one placeMore complex architecture to build
Decision
Concept C — the unified workspace. It best supported the primary find→understand→act loop and kept giving, timeline, and actions in one context. Trade-off: a more complex architecture — paid back by the design system, which made the complexity reusable.
09 — INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE

Restructured around the real org model

Atlas ├─ Dashboard (role-aware "what needs me today") ├─ Donors → Donor Workspace: Overview · Timeline · Giving · Communications · Campaign log ├─ Gifts & Pledges (entry, batch, receipting) ├─ Campaigns → Funds · Appeals ├─ Reports (builder · saved views · viewer) ├─ Pipeline · Tasks · Communications · Events · Volunteers ├─ Intelligence → Guru AI · Analytics └─ Admin → Users & Roles · Tags · Integrations · Smart Triggers · Sync · Location Portal (legal entities)

The key structural change: the diocese is a federation of legal entities, so the whole product is scoped to that hierarchy (Location Portal), and the donor became a workspace rather than a chain of separate pages.

10 — USER FLOW

Before → after

Before

Search ↓ Donor list ↓ Profile ↓ back ↓ Payments ↓ back ↓ Timeline ↓ Action

After

Search ↓ Donor Workspace
  ├─ Overview
  ├─ Timeline
  ├─ Giving
  └─ Actions

The redesign consolidated related information into one contextual workspace, collapsing a 7-step back-and-forth into a single destination.

11 — WIREFRAMES & ITERATIONS

Three iterations that mattered

Iteration 01 — everything, everywhere. First pass put all donor data on one screen. Too much; users couldn't find the priority. ↓Iteration 02 — better hierarchy, weak actions. Cleaned the hierarchy but the "next action" got buried. ↓Iteration 03 — context + action. Priority items and actions surface first; depth (timeline, giving) sits one tab away but in the same workspace.

The value isn't the wireframes — it's the why behind each change: from "show everything" to "show what enables the next action."

12 — DESIGN DECISIONS

The calls I'd defend

Decision 01 · Prioritize actionable information
Problem: users couldn't quickly see what needed attention. Decision: surface priority items (overdue tasks, lapsing donors, pledges due) above secondary metrics. Trade-off: less data visible at first glance — accepted, because the primary goal is action, not reporting.
Decision 02 · Keep context visible
Problem: constant page-to-page navigation. Decision: contextual panels and a unified workspace so giving, history, and actions stay together. Trade-off: higher information density — managed with hierarchy and the type scale.
Decision 03 · Separate identity from financials
Problem: cross-entity privacy vs. findability. Decision: global donor search, but gift/payment detail gated to the viewer's entity, shown as a clear locked state. Trade-off: a visible "locked" state — chosen over a confusing blank.
Decision 04 · Add intelligence, keep humans deciding
Problem: insight buried in data. Decision: Guru AI surfaces grounded, explainable insights and answers; it never acts on money by itself. Trade-off: AI does less autonomously — the right call for trust.
13 — DESIGN SYSTEM

Constellation — the system that made 18 modules possible

None of this scales without a system. I built Constellation from the ground up: a three-tier token foundation (primitive → semantic → component) and a reusable kit, so every module is assembled from one language and a change at the token layer updates the whole product.

Foundations: color (semantic status), typography (DM Serif for data, DM Sans for UI), spacing & radius units, elevation. Components: buttons, inputs, filter chips, tables, KPI cards, tags/status, drawers, modals, tabs, charts. Advanced: tokens & variables, explicit states (empty, loading, gated, error), and a consistent dark-chrome + light-content theme.

14 — ACCESSIBILITY

Considered, not claimed

Accessibility was designed for (not formally audited): color-contrast-aware semantic tokens, keyboard navigation and visible focus states, explicit error and empty states, clear form labels, and adequate touch targets on the mobile companion. I don't claim formal WCAG compliance — it wasn't validated.

15 — FINAL SOLUTION

The product, told as a story

01 · Donor workspace — context in one place

02 · Donors — a forgiving, scannable list

03 · Location Portal — the multi-entity backbone

04 · Reports — self-serve, repeatable

05 · Guru AI — ask in plain English

16 — PROTOTYPE / INTERACTION

One query, end to end

The signature interaction: a plain-English question becomes a working list you can act on — open a profile, generate a report, or send outreach, without leaving the page.

1 · Ask → the right donors
2 · Open anyone for full context
3 · Act — report or outreach
The loop closes itself: sending outreach logs the contact and refreshes the donor's record, so the next answer is always current.
17 — COLLABORATION

How I worked with the team

Product

Aligned user needs with business priorities; sequenced what shipped first.

Engineering

Mapped every token to a CSS variable and checked component feasibility early.

Research / stakeholders

Used feedback and support themes to validate key workflows.

Design

Established reusable patterns so new modules inherit the system for free.

18 — IMPACT

Product outcomes

The project was a design-led platform redesign; quantitative metrics weren't available at this stage, so I report legitimate product outcomes rather than invented numbers.

  • Reduced workflow complexity — a 7-step donor loop collapsed into one workspace
  • Consolidated multiple separate workflows into contextual surfaces
  • Improved information hierarchy across the product
  • Created a reusable component system (Constellation) spanning 18 modules
  • Established a scalable, token-based architecture and cleaner developer handoff
Honest note: impact measurement wasn't available because the work was still in development. The next step is to instrument and measure (below).
19 — WHAT I'D DO NEXT

If we had another iteration

  1. Validate the redesigned workflow with more real users
  2. Instrument and measure task completion, time-on-task, and report self-serve rate
  3. Explore role-based personalization of the dashboard and workspace
  4. Deepen mobile/responsive behavior beyond the field companion
20 — REFLECTION

What I learned

The hardest part wasn't reducing the number of screens — it was deciding which information users needed at each moment, so the workspace felt focused instead of crowded.

What I'd do differently: involve engineering even earlier during the IA exploration, to surface implementation constraints (especially around the multi-entity data model) before committing to a direction.

Thank you for reading.
